A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same AdaWorld research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V1 reports original action-transfer, simulation, visual-planning, ablation, and action-clustering results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluations, continuous-action simulation, robot planning, and additional analyses.

M1.justification: V1 adapts discrete controls by averaging latent actions into action embeddings. V2 Section 2.3 adds an MLP mapping continuous raw actions into the latent-action interface, initialized using action–latent-action pairs. This extends the adaptation procedure while retaining the core autoencoder, diffusion model, and training objectives.

E1.justification: V2 adds nuScenes continuous-action driving simulation, VP2 robot planning with Robosuite and RoboDesk, and BAIR robot-pushing evaluation. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the retained action-transfer, discrete-action simulation, and game-planning tasks. The original pretraining data mixture remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 Table 6 newly evaluates iVideoGPT against an action-aware iVideoGPT variant. The original action-agnostic, optical-flow, discrete-latent-action, and game-planning comparator sets remain intact; extending existing comparators to nuScenes does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include four volunteers judging 50 video pairs per action-transfer dataset, continuous-control adaptation, and MPPI robot planning using a low-resolution model with 1,000 adaptation steps. Appendix B.6 adds 27,000 continuation-pretraining steps, 1,000 BAIR finetuning steps, and evaluation on 256 videos. The existing discrete-simulation and Procgen protocols are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a backbone-generality test using iVideoGPT and a UMAP analysis comparing beta values of 0.0002 and 0.00002. It also extends initialization and adaptation-efficiency analyses to nuScenes. These address architecture dependence and latent-action disentanglement beyond the retained data-diversity, clustering, and failure-case analyses.

E5.justification: V2 newly specifies four runs per VP2 task with standard errors. Procgen retains the stated five-seed, standard-error reporting protocol. Its changed error values do not establish additional runs or a changed estimator and are assessed under E6.

E6.justification: V2 adds human transfer scores, nuScenes results, VP2 planning outcomes, and BAIR comparisons. Examples include AdaWorld's human success rates of 70.5% on LIBERO and 61.5% on SSv2, and BAIR PSNR/LPIPS of 17.40/0.204 for action-aware iVideoGPT versus 16.59/0.220 for iVideoGPT. Existing benchmark means remain unchanged, but Table 3 revises uncertainty values: finetuned AdaWorld's average changes from 56.67±0.44% to 56.67±2.16%.

T1.justification: The VAE, beta-VAE, and diffusion objectives in Equations 1–3 are unchanged. V2 adds empirical analysis and procedural explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central claims: action-aware pretraining enables transferable latent actions, efficient adaptation, and improved simulation and planning. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the iVideoGPT experiment as evidence of applicability across architectures and explains UMAP noise through actions that cannot execute in particular states. It also acknowledges that Flat block and Open drawer produce no meaningful scores under constrained adaptation and omits them from Table 4. The original limitations and failure-case discussion remain.

D1.justification: V2 discloses 300-sample validation sets, a two-layer continuous-action MLP trained for 3,000 steps, and its runtime. New Appendices B.5–B.6 document robot trajectory counts, adaptation hyperparameters, and iVideoGPT checkpoint and frozen-tokenizer choices. These targeted additions supplement unchanged core architecture, pretraining, sampling, and project-access information.

R1.justification: The retained related-work discussion adds citations including DriveGAN, MotionClone, Space-Time Diffusion Features, and PreLAR. References supporting the new benchmarks, planning procedure, and UMAP analysis are also added. The positioning relative to passive-video pretraining and discrete latent actions remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 4 to Appendix F, and the conclusion is renumbered. V2 separates game and robot planning, expands adaptation explanations, renames the ablation section, and makes localized wording and affiliation edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation: Figure 1 is redesigned with robot-planning results, Table 1 gains human-evaluation columns, and Table 2 and Figure 6 incorporate nuScenes. New robot-planning and iVideoGPT tables and a UMAP figure are added. Appendix displays are retained across renumbering, while the data-mixture table gains an automated-generation column.

improvement.justification: V1's quantitative adaptation and planning evidence centered on discrete controls and games. V2 substantially strengthens the broad adaptability claim through continuous-control simulation, robot planning, and a second world-model architecture. Human judgments and the beta analysis also strengthen evaluation and design justification. Omitted low-scoring robot tasks and unexplained Procgen error revisions remain weaknesses, but the new controlled comparisons materially improve the paper's evidential foundation.
